clue.text: Look into big cuts in wet weather wear

indicators.note: the word 'into' tells us one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: big cuts are gashes
lo is an old word for look or behold

explanation.surface: Someone is told to inspect deep wounds while wearing rainwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Galoshes are rubber overshoes worn to keep shoes dry in rain or slush.

clue.text: His sporting ambition to be good for nothing?

definitions.text: His sporting ambition to be good for nothing?

parts.words: His sporting ambition to be good for nothing
parts.note: not a layabout but a sportsman who wants to excel without being paid

explanation.walkthrough: 'good for nothing' looks like an insult but means skilled while playing unpaid.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-professional player takes part in sport without payment.

clue.text: Old man Flanagan's valet looks into complaints

parts.note: OM is an abbreviation of old man
Bud Flanagan was a British comedian of Flanagan and Allen, so Flanagan's gives Bud's
a valet is a manservant, a man

explanation.surface: An elderly comedian's manservant investigates grievances.
explanation.walkthrough: Bud Flanagan was a mid-century British music-hall comedian; his first name gives BUD'S.
explanation.definitionFit: An ombudsman is an official who investigates grievances against organisations.

clue.text: Damage includes the French quarter of New York

indicators.note: includes means one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: to harm is to damage
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Destruction reaches the French district of a big American city.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlem is a district in northern Manhattan.

clue.text: Four-thirty being one of these current indicators ?

definitions.text: Four-thirty being one of these current indicators ?

parts.words: Four-thirty being one of these current indicators
parts.note: a clock reading shows the hour, so a clock showing half past four is an indication of the present moment

explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally, '4.30' is a sign of the time; the phrase means features that typify the present age.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names trends that reveal the character of the present day.

clue.text: With hands thus kept warm, missed the catch

explanation.surface: A fielder with cosy hands drops the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Hands kept in a muff are muffed, and to muff a catch is to fumble and drop it.

clue.text: Mr French is the principal trouble-maker

parts.note: M is the abbreviation of Monsieur, French for Mr
the principal or head person is the chief

explanation.surface: A Frenchman turns out to be the ringleader of the troublemakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Mischief is harm or a cause of trouble, and the word was once used of a person who causes it.

clue.text: US pioneer express-man holds the academician, Jumble

indicators.note: holds means one piece contains the other

parts.note: William Fargo co-founded the Wells Fargo express company in the American West
RA stands for Royal Academician

explanation.surface: An American stagecoach pioneer carries an artist in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: William Fargo was a founder of the Wells Fargo stagecoach and express business in the nineteenth-century American West.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrago is a confused mixture or hotchpotch.

clue.text: Made out record on eagle having died

parts.note: a record is a disc
an erne is a sea eagle

explanation.surface: Someone spotted a record placed on a dead eagle.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something out is to perceive or detect it.

clue.text: The bend of the road

parts.note: not a curve along the route but the slight sideways arch built across a road surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'bend' suggests a corner, but the clue means the curve of the road's cross-section that lets rain run off.
explanation.definitionFit: A road's camber is its convex shaping from crown to kerb so water drains away.

clue.text: Supplier of fuel advertises its effectiveness

explanation.surface: A fuel company promotes how well its product performs.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as 'gas works', the phrase is a claim that the gas is effective.
explanation.definitionFit: A gasworks is a plant producing town gas for supply; read as a sentence, it boasts that the gas does its job.

clue.text: It appears that this is a hat — unworn ?

definitions.text: It appears that this is a hat — unworn ?

parts.words: It appears that this is a hat — unworn
parts.note: a hat sitting on nothing looks as though no one, not even a head, is under it

explanation.walkthrough: The picture is of a hat lying unworn, seemingly lacking the part of the body that would fill it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking a head describes a hat with nobody wearing it, as if its wearer had none.

clue.text: A chore perhaps for a Sabine farmer

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters given might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A farm task waits for a farmer in the Sabine hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges A CHORE. The Roman poet Horace was given a farm in the Sabine hills by his patron Maecenas.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman poet famously owned and wrote about his farm in the Sabine country near Rome.

clue.text: Creditor has some current problem for a writer

parts.note: CR is the accounting abbreviation for creditor
an amp is a unit, an amount, of electric current

explanation.surface: A lender has electrical trouble that bothers an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Writer's cramp is a painful spasm of the hand from long spells of handwriting.

clue.text: Bob we bear is from an army establishment over a river

parts.note: an army camp is a military establishment
the Nile is the river of Egypt

explanation.surface: A man called Bob is said to come from a military camp across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' is not a man but a bell-ringing term for a change rung on bells; it is heard from a bell tower.
explanation.definitionFit: A campanile is a bell tower, where bell changes such as a bob are rung.

clue.text: Time for lotos-eating, apparently

parts.note: Tennyson's Lotos-Eaters reach a land at a particular hour of the day, a land where that hour seemed endless

explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's poem 'The Lotos-Eaters' begins 'In the afternoon they came unto a land / In which it seemed always afternoon.'
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson places the sailors' arrival and their dreamy idleness in the period after midday.

clue.text: Terrible fellow raised gun, or was it Henry?

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means a piece is written upwards

parts.note: Ivan the Terrible was a tsar of Russia
gat is slang for a gun

explanation.surface: A fearsome man lifts a weapon, or was it a king named Henry?
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns IVAN upwards to NAVI. Prince Henry of Portugal sponsored voyages of discovery and is called the Navigator.
explanation.definitionFit: Portugal's Prince Henry is known by the epithet given to sea explorers who steer ships.

clue.text: Pay through the mouth?

parts.note: suggests paying through the nose, but means bringing something out through the mouth, or handing back something taken

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'pay through the nose' is the false trail; to disgorge is to spew out, or to give up ill-gotten gains.
explanation.definitionFit: To disgorge is to eject from the throat, and figuratively to surrender money unwillingly.

clue.text: Sweet sleeper on a bank at Belmont

definitions.text: Sweet sleeper on a bank at Belmont

parts.words: Sweet sleeper on a bank at Belmont
parts.note: a quotation from The Merchant of Venice, set at Portia's house Belmont, where the night light rests on a grassy slope

explanation.walkthrough: Lorenzo says in The Merchant of Venice 'How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank!' at Belmont; 'bank' is a grassy slope, not a lender.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare pictures the night's lunar glow lying asleep on a bank in Portia's garden.

clue.text: Not even meant, we hear, as a casual thing

parts.note: an odd number is not even

indicators.note: we hear means the next word is taken by its sound

parts.note: said aloud, these words sound like MENT

explanation.surface: Something said in passing was not meant in earnest.
explanation.definitionFit: An oddment is a stray leftover item, something of chance rather than design.

clue.text: Like the egg of a duck eaten by a Latin poet

indicators.note: eaten by means one piece is swallowed inside another

parts.note: Ovid was a Latin poet, author of the Metamorphoses
a duck is a zero score in cricket, so the letter O

explanation.surface: A Roman poet dines on a duck egg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eaten by' puts O (duck, cricket's nought) inside OVID.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovoid means egg-shaped, from the Latin word for egg.

clue.text: Confines these US doctors to hospital ?

explanation.surface: Junior American doctors are kept penned up in the hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: To intern is to detain or confine; American junior hospital doctors are also called by this name.

clue.text: Sound advice to architect of such a heavenly body

indicators.note: sound tells us to go by how the phrase is spoken

parts.note: the advice to an architect would be to draw up a design for it

explanation.surface: A designer gets solid advice on a celestial building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' says the advice 'plan it' is taken by how it is spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: A planet is a large body orbiting a star, such as Mars.

clue.text: Description of Hardy's crowd, 11, just putting it on

indicators.note: the clue refers to the answer at 11 across, meaning without a head, so the first letter goes

parts.note: Thomas Hardy's novel is Far from the Madding Crowd, so madding describes the crowd

explanation.surface: A remark about a novelist's crowd turns out to be mere affectation.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' borrows that answer, headless, as the instruction: MADDING loses its first letter M.
explanation.definitionFit: Adding is putting something on, increasing an amount.

clue.text: Poor wayfarers tend to get all bothered here ?

definitions.text: Poor wayfarers tend to get all bothered here ?

indicators.note: bothered means flustered, so these letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: Penniless travellers grow flustered at a certain roadside point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bothered' rearranges TO GET ALL. A poor traveller is upset at the barrier where a road charge must be paid.
explanation.definitionFit: A tollgate is a barrier where travellers must pay a fee to pass.

clue.text: Sign representing dog that is being worried by a sheep

indicators.note: worried, like a sheepdog worrying its flock, means the letters are harried into a new order

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A notice shows a dog being harassed by a sheep, a reversal of the usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being worried' rearranges DOG plus IE to give IDEOG, followed by RAM.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideogram is a written symbol standing for an idea rather than a sound.

clue.text: Dame's disposition

parts.note: Dame is the personified natural world, and one's disposition or temperament shares her name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dame' is the personification often called Dame or Mother Nature; a person's character is also their nature.
explanation.definitionFit: Character or temperament is called one's nature, and the personified world is Dame Nature.

clue.text: How may we say this dish is brought in ?

definitions.text: How may we say this dish is brought in ?

parts.words: How may we say this dish is brought in
parts.note: the dish's French name also means coming in, an entry

explanation.walkthrough: The French word for a course of a meal also means 'entrance', so the dish name describes its being brought in.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrée is a course of a meal, and in French the word means entry.

clue.text: South African race Includes girl 12 for instance

indicators.note: includes means the second piece is held within the first

parts.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
Iris is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A race in South Africa admits a young woman, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: The '12' points to the answer at 12 across, the Roman poet Horace, who wrote satires.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman poet wrote Satires, so he exemplifies a writer of mockery.
